personnel_record.notes: TWO sessions. January 18, 1959 (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack, NJ): McLean's first session as a Blue Note leader; quintet with Donald Byrd, Sonny Clark (piano on Blues Inn and Fidel only, absent on Quadrangle), Paul Chambers, Philly Joe Jones. September 1, 1960 (Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ): sextet with Blue Mitchell, Tina Brooks, Kenny Drew, Paul Chambers, Art Taylor. SESSION-DATE CONFLICT vs. task brief: the dispatch premise (Jan 19, 1959 with Blue Mitchell/Tina Brooks/Kenny Drew/Philly Joe Jones; Sep 18, 1959 with Hank Mobley/Louis Hayes) is contradicted by ALL four consulted sources — Wikipedia, jazzdisco.org, Discogs, and AllMusic — which unanimously give Jan 18, 1959 and Sep 1, 1960 with the rosters recorded here. Hank Mobley and Louis Hayes appear on NO source for this album and are not included; the brief's premise appears to conflate other McLean sessions. RELEASE-YEAR CONFLICT: AllMusic dates the album 1960; Wikipedia gives release June 1961; Discogs first pressing 1961 (BLP 4051). The 1960 in the canonical ID follows the AllMusic/project convention. CD reissue adds three bonus tracks (Street Singer, Melonae's Dance, Medina) from the same Sep 1, 1960 session — excluded from the original-LP track list here. Engineer Rudy Van Gelder is listed on the AllMusic credits page (obs). Producer Alfred Lion per Wikipedia infobox and Blue Note practice of the period. Per-musician track coverage is source-confirmed (jazzdisco per-take rosters plus Wikipedia personnel-by-track-group), so track_assignments_complete is true for the original six LP tracks.

ballot.case_for: Session gravity is the album's strongest signal: two Blue Note dates staffed with A-list hard boppers — the January 1959 quintet (Donald Byrd, Sonny Clark, Paul Chambers, Philly Joe Jones) marking McLean's first session as a Blue Note leader, and the September 1960 sextet (Blue Mitchell, Tina Brooks, Kenny Drew, Chambers, Art Taylor) cut the same day as material for Brooks's Back to the Tracks. 'Appointment in Ghana' is McLean's most-covered composition and a post-bop repertoire staple, while the pianoless 'Quadrangle' audibly documents the stretch from Parker-rooted hard bop toward the freedoms of Let Freedom Ring (1962). Side B doubles as a rare window into the historically undervalued Tina Brooks as both writer and player. Sourcing is above the floor: six sources, four convergent on the contested points, per-track personnel complete.
ballot.case_against: Neither reference rates this among McLean's defining statements — the titles consensus lists actually carry are Let Freedom Ring, One Step Beyond, and Destination... Out!, and Jackie's Bag rarely commands their core-collection status, lacking even the single-session unity of Bluesnik. It is an assembled patchwork: two sessions twenty months apart in two different studios, different front lines and rhythm sections with only Paul Chambers common to both, its cohesion editorial (Alfred Lion's compilation) rather than organic. It also enters the most densely canonicalized two-year stretch in post-bop as a solid contributor rather than an indispensable node, and its strongest evidence — the Brooks sextet — is partly evidence for Back to the Tracks rather than for this LP alone.
ballot.recommendation: John should hear it as a contested depth-add — weighing whether McLean's canon presence is better founded on a unified single-session statement (Let Freedom Ring or One Step Beyond) if he is not yet represented — and if included, footnote the 1960 (AllMusic) vs. 1961 (Wikipedia/Discogs) release-year conflict in the canon row.
